analysis.one_liner: Requires big political spenders to reveal their donors and closes loopholes letting foreign money into elections.
analysis.headline: Backed by 193 House Democrats and no Republicans, the DISCLOSE Act was sent to three committees and never received a single vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The DISCLOSE Act would require corporations, unions, super PACs, and tax-exempt "dark money" groups that spend more than $10,000 on elections to report that spending to the Federal Election Commission within 24 hours, and to name donors who gave $10,000 or more. Political ads would have to name their biggest funders on screen or on air. It would also extend the existing ban on foreign money in elections to digital ads, ballot initiatives, and campaigns around federal judgeship nominations, with criminal penalties for hiding foreign money through shell companies. The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters gain the right to know who is paying for the political ads they see before they cast a ballot, including ads for and against Supreme Court and other federal judgeship nominees, which today can be run with no disclosure at all. Voters also gain stronger enforcement of the ban on foreign money, which currently can slip in through web ads, ballot initiatives, and shell companies. Candidates and campaigns facing undisclosed attack ads benefit from a more level information field.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, who learn who funds election ads

how_it_helps.text: Organizations spending more than $10,000 on elections must report it to the FEC within 24 hours and disclose donors who gave $10,000 or more, under penalty of perjury, so voters can trace spending to its source before Election Day.

Political ads must carry a spoken or on-screen statement of who is paying, plus a list of the organization's top funders, so viewers see the money behind the message rather than just a generic committee name.

The bill extends the ban on foreign money to paid digital and web communications, ballot initiatives and referenda, and communications about federal judicial nominations, and makes it a crime punishable by up to five years in prison to set up a company for the purpose of hiding a foreign national's election spending.

It requires disclosure of spending on campaigns for and against federal judicial nominees, a category the bill's findings note has drawn hundreds of millions of dollars in undisclosed spending, including nearly $40 million from a single group on Supreme Court nominees since 2016.

analysis.who_pays: Dark money organizations, major undisclosed donors, and corporations and unions that spend on elections lose their ability to influence campaigns anonymously. They would bear new reporting obligations, 24-hour deadlines, and compliance costs, and their big donors would be named publicly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Dark money groups and major undisclosed donors

drawbacks.text: The reporting threshold is low: any covered organization spending just over $10,000 in a two-year election cycle must file FEC reports and identify its large donors, which sweeps in small advocacy groups and nonprofits and imposes real paperwork and legal compliance costs on them.

Naming an ad's top funders and reporting large donors can deter people from supporting controversial causes, which is why the bill itself requires an FEC regulation for the exception it creates for donors facing serious threats, harassment, or reprisals, and requires rules consistent with the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision.
The disclosure duties fall on labor unions and tax-exempt organizations as well as corporations, so unions and issue groups lose the same spending anonymity that corporate-funded groups lose.

The bill depends on the Federal Election Commission to write and enforce the rules, and the FEC's partisan structure means enforcement of campaign finance law is often slow or deadlocked, so disclosure rules can exist on paper while violations go unpunished.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: voters get timely, traceable information about who is bankrolling the ads trying to persuade them, in exchange for compliance costs on organizations that spend money in elections. The strongest honest objections are the low $10,000 threshold, which burdens small groups, and the possibility that naming top funders chills lawful political giving. The bill does include a harassment exemption and carve-outs for ordinary business funds, which blunts but does not eliminate those concerns. Enforcement ultimately rests on an FEC that is often deadlocked, so the bill's practical value would depend on rules and staffing that Congress did not guarantee. On balance, the bill targets a real information gap that current law leaves open, especially around judicial nominations and foreign money, and its burdens fall mainly on large spenders.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or floor time; it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Representative David Cicilline introduced the DISCLOSE Act on February 21, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Administration, Ways and Means, and Judiciary committees, with the timing of any consideration left to the Speaker.
The bill gathered 193 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat, with no Republican support.
The only action after referral was procedural: in July 2023, Representative Chris Pappas took over as first sponsor so cosponsors could continue to be added and reprints requested.
The House Administration Committee, the primary committee of referral, never held a markup or vote, and the full House never debated or voted on the bill at any point in the two-year Congress.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the bill still sitting in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Dark money organizations, undisclosed major donors, and groups spending anonymously on judicial nominations are better off: they kept the ability to influence elections and courts without revealing their funders, and voters never received the disclosure rights the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Dark money groups and undisclosed donors

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.role: Lead sponsor, House Judiciary Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the DISCLOSE Act and recruited an initial bloc of more than 100 Democratic cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 193 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill, all of the support it attracted in the House.

for.name: Rep. Chris Pappas
for.what_they_did: Asked to be treated as first sponsor in July 2023 so cosponsor additions and reprintings could continue after the original sponsor.

against.name: House Republican leadership (Speaker of the House)
against.what_they_did: Structured the referral to three committees at once with consideration timing left to the Speaker, and never brought the bill to the floor for a vote during the entire Congress.

against.name: House Administration Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the primary committee of referral (Bryan Steil, R-WI)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; no committee action appears anywhere in the two-year action history.

sides.party_line_note: All 193 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; with Republicans holding the House majority and controlling committees and floor scheduling, the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.industry: Dark money groups and 501(c)(4) tax-exempt organizations
industries.note: These groups could keep spending on elections but would have to file FEC reports within 24 hours and name donors of $10,000 or more, ending the anonymity that made 'dark money' possible. Their interest in concealing funders runs directly against voters' interest in knowing who is behind the ads.

Donors giving $10,000 or more to election-spending organizations would be named, and setting up a corporation to hide foreign election money would become a crime carrying up to five years in prison. Concealment, which is the point of many such vehicles, would no longer be available.

industries.industry: Corporations and labor unions spending on politics
industries.note: Both remain free to spend under the bill but must report disbursements over $1,000 and identify large funders. The burden is symmetric, though the loss of anonymity weighs differently on each side's spending strategies.

industries.industry: Large digital platforms and political ad networks
industries.note: Platforms with 50 million or more monthly U.S. users must carry expanded disclaimers, including top-funder lists, on political ads, a compliance cost but not a prohibition. Platforms profit from political advertising volume, so added friction runs against their business interest even though the public gains transparency.
